1.title: The Birth of Solid-State Electronics
1.text:
The Birth of Solid-State Electronics

Solid-state devices are made of semiconducting materials that amplify and control weak electric signals through electron movement inside a tiny crystal.

Our big question for this lesson: how are semiconductors manipulated to make electronic components? Every electronic device traces its roots to the vacuum tubes of the early 1900s. In a vacuum tube, electron beams flow through empty space to amplify and control faint electric signals. But tubes are big, need lots of power, and give off lots of thermal energy. Their heated filaments burn out, so tubes had to be replaced every one to five years.

In the late 1940s, solid-state devices made of semiconductors were invented to do the same jobs. They control signals by moving electrons inside a tiny crystal. Very few electrons flow, and there's no filament, so they need little power, make little heat, are tiny and cheap, and last 20 years or more.

A decade later, these devices were combined with other components into the first integrated circuit, built in 1958 and shown in Figure 9. Its strip of germanium is about 1 centimeter long. Today's phones, TVs, and laptops rely on semiconductor devices packed onto silicon chips a few millimeters wide. In them, current and potential difference behave in ways more complex than Ohm's law, and they can convert AC to DC and amplify potential differences.

3.title: Diodes and the Depletion Layer
3.text:
Diodes and the Depletion Layer

A pn-junction diode is a sandwich of p-type and n-type semiconductor; the region around the junction with no charge carriers is the depletion layer.

The simplest semiconductor device is the diode, a sandwich of p-type and n-type semiconductor, as in Figure 10. To make one, a single piece of silicon is treated first with a p-dopant and then with an n-dopant. The boundary between the two sides is the junction, so this is a pn-junction diode. Metal contacts on each end let you attach wires.

Free electrons on the n-side are attracted to the holes on the p-side, so they cross over and recombine with holes. Holes from the p-side likewise move over and recombine with electrons. This leaves the n-side with a net positive charge and the p-side with a net negative charge. Those charges push back and stop any further flow.

The region around the junction now has neither holes nor free electrons. It's called the depletion layer, and with no charge carriers, it's a poor conductor. So a diode is two pretty good conductors wrapped around a poor one.

4.title: Forward and Reverse Bias
4.text:
Forward and Reverse Bias

A reverse-biased diode acts as a very high-value resistor; a forward-biased diode acts as a low-value resistor.

Hook up a diode the way shown on the left of Figure 10, with the battery's positive terminal on the n-side. Both the electrons in the n-type material and the holes in the p-type material are pulled toward the battery terminals, away from the junction. The depletion layer gets wider, no charge carriers meet, and almost no current flows. The diode is nearly an insulator. This is a reverse-biased diode.

Flip the battery around, as on the right of Figure 10, and charge carriers move toward the junction. If the potential difference is big enough, 0.6 volts for a silicon diode, electrons reach the p-end and fill the holes. The depletion layer vanishes and current flows. The battery keeps supplying electrons to the n-end and removing them from the p-end, which is the same as supplying holes. This is a forward-biased diode.

The arrow in the diode symbol points the way conventional current is allowed through.

5.title: Diode Current and Rectifiers
5.text:
Diode Current and Rectifiers

A rectifier is a diode used to convert alternating current to direct current, acting like a one-way door.

Figure 11 graphs the current through a silicon diode against the potential difference across it. When the potential difference is negative, the diode is reverse-biased and acts like a huge resistor. Only a tiny current, about ten to the negative eleventh amperes, gets through.

When the potential difference is positive, the diode is forward-biased. Below about 0.6 volts, there's still almost no current. Above that threshold, the current shoots up, and the diode acts like a low-value resistor. Raising the potential difference raises the current, but not in the straight-line way Ohm's law predicts. A typical diode has about 0.7 volts across it when it conducts.

A big use for diodes is turning alternating current into direct current. The diode works like a one-way door for charge. A diode used this way is called a rectifier.

6.title: Example Problem 4, A Diode in a Simple Circuit
6.text:
Example Problem 4, A Diode in a Simple Circuit

By Kirchhoff's law, the supply's potential difference equals I R plus the potential difference across the diode.

A 0.70 volt silicon diode, like the one in Figure 11, is connected to a power supply through a 470 ohm resistor. The supply forward-biases the diode and is adjusted until the diode current is 12 milliamperes. What potential difference does the power supply produce?

Step one: analyze and sketch the problem. Draw a circuit with the diode, the 470 ohm resistor, and the power supply, and show the direction of current. Knowns: I is 0.012 amperes, the diode's potential difference is 0.70 volts, and R is 470 ohms. Unknown: the supply's potential difference.

Step two: solve for the unknown. The potential difference across the resistor comes from delta V equals I R. By Kirchhoff's law, the supply's potential difference is the sum of the potential differences across the resistor and the diode. So it's 0.012 amperes times 470 ohms, plus 0.70 volts. That's 5.64 volts plus 0.70 volts, or 6.3 volts.

Step three: evaluate the answer. The answer is in volts, which is right for a potential difference. And the size fits the current and resistance.

7.title: Light-Emitting Diodes
7.text:
Light-Emitting Diodes

A light-emitting diode, or LED, releases energy as light when electrons and holes recombine at its forward-biased junction.

Diodes made from certain mixes of elements, like gallium and aluminum with arsenic and phosphorus, glow when they're forward-biased. When electrons reach the holes at the junction, they recombine and release their extra energy as light. These are light-emitting diodes, or LEDs. You'll find them as indicator lights on computers, in display signs, traffic lights, and lamps. They're bright, cool, and extremely efficient.

Diodes can detect light, too. Light falling on the junction of a reverse-biased diode creates electrons and holes, producing a current that depends on how bright the light is. And to make an LED light up, the battery's positive terminal goes to the p-end, so the diode is forward-biased.

8.title: Diode Lasers
8.text:
Diode Lasers

A diode laser is an LED configured to emit a beam of coherent, monochromatic laser light.

Some LEDs are built to emit a beam of coherent, monochromatic laser light. These diode lasers are cheap, compact, and powerful. They're used in optical disc players, laser pointers, and bar-code scanners like the one in Figure 12, which both shines light and detects the light bouncing back from the bars.

A typical diode laser emits light at about 800 nanometers, in the near infrared. The beam comes from a tiny spot on a gallium-aluminum-arsenic chip. Running on 80 milliamperes, the diode has a forward potential difference of about 2 volts.

9.title: Transistors
9.text:
Transistors

A transistor is a device made of doped semiconductor layers, a base between an emitter and a collector, that can amplify currents.

A transistor is made of doped semiconductor and can amplify currents. One type, the npn-transistor, has n-type layers on either side of a thin p-type layer, as in Figure 13. The pnp-transistor is the same idea flipped. The middle layer is the base, and the outer regions are the emitter and the collector.

Figure 13 also shows the schematic symbols. The arrow on the emitter shows the direction of conventional current. In an npn-transistor it points away from the base, and in a pnp-transistor it points toward the base.

10.title: Amplification
10.text:
Amplification

Current gain is the ratio of the collector current to the base current, I sub C over I sub B.

Figure 14 shows an npn-transistor amplifying current. Think of its two pn-junctions as two diodes back to back. With only the right battery, V sub C, connected, the collector is more positive than the emitter. The base-collector diode is reverse-biased with a wide depletion layer, so no current flows from collector to base. Connect the left battery, V sub B, and the base becomes more positive than the emitter. The base-emitter diode is forward-biased, and a base current, I sub B, flows from base to emitter.

The very thin base is part of both diodes. Charges injected by I sub B reduce the reverse bias of the base-collector diode, letting charge flow between collector and emitter. So a small change in I sub B makes a big change in the collector current, I sub C, perhaps 100 times bigger. That current creates a potential difference across resistor R sub C, so small changes in the base potential become large changes in output.

The ratio I sub C over I sub B is the current gain, a handy measure of a transistor's performance. For general-purpose transistors it ranges from 50 to 300. A pnp-transistor works the same way, with both batteries reversed.

11.title: Transistors as Switches
11.text:
Transistors as Switches

In computers, small base-emitter currents switch large collector-emitter currents on and off.

In computers, transistors are usually not amplifiers but super-fast switches. A small current in the base-emitter circuit turns a large current in the collector-emitter circuit on or off.

Connect several transistors together, and they can perform logic operations or even add numbers. Billions of these on-off decisions every second are what let a computer think in ones and zeros.

12.title: Integrated Circuits
12.text:
Integrated Circuits

An integrated circuit, or microchip, combines many transistors, diodes, resistors, and conductors, each less than a micrometer across, on one piece of silicon.

An integrated circuit, called a microchip, holds huge numbers of transistors, diodes, resistors, and conductors, each less than a micrometer across. All of them can be made by doping silicon with donor or acceptor atoms.

A microchip starts as an extremely pure single crystal of silicon, 10 to 30 centimeters across and 1 to 2 meters long. A diamond-coated saw slices it into wafers less than 1 millimeter thick, as in the left photo of Figure 15. Then the circuit is built layer by layer on the wafer's surface.

13.title: Building a Chip Layer by Layer
13.text:
Building a Chip Layer by Layer

Chips are made by covering a wafer with a patterned protective layer and exposing the uncovered areas to dopants, oxygen, or aluminum vapor.

Using a photographic process, most of the wafer is covered with a protective layer, leaving a pattern of open spots to be doped. In a vacuum chamber, vapors of a dopant like arsenic dope the open regions. By controlling the exposure, engineers control how well those regions conduct. This makes resistors, or one layer of a diode or transistor.

Then the protective layer comes off, a new pattern goes on, and the wafer is exposed to another dopant, often gallium, making pn-junctions. A third layer can form npn-transistors. Exposing the wafer to oxygen makes silicon dioxide insulation. Finally, aluminum vapor lays down thin conducting pathways between components. Why aluminum and not gallium or arsenic? Aluminum is a metal and a good conductor on its own, while gallium and arsenic are dopants that only change how a semiconductor conducts. The right photo in Figure 15 shows a finished wafer.

14.title: STEM Career Connection, Materials Engineer
14.text:
STEM Career Connection, Materials Engineer

Materials engineers use the properties and structures of materials to create new materials for products such as computer chips.

Love figuring out what things are made of? Materials engineers must understand the properties and structures of all kinds of materials, like metals, plastics, and nanomaterials. They use that knowledge to create new materials a product might need, from computer chips to aerospace parts to biomedical devices.

Many materials engineers work at universities or in research and development labs.

15.title: Computing and Microchips
15.text:
Computing and Microchips

Miniaturized microchips increase the processing speed, functionality, and reliability of computers.

Thousands of identical circuits, called chips, are made at once on a single wafer. They're tested, sliced apart, mounted in a carrier, wired to contacts, and sealed in a protective plastic case. Since signals only travel tiny distances, complicated circuits fit in a small space, like the central processing unit in Figure 16. Miniaturization has made computers faster, more capable, and more reliable, and chips now run appliances and cars too.

Making semiconductor electronics takes teamwork. Physicists understand how electrons and holes move. Physicists and chemists together add precise amounts of dopants to ultra-pure silicon. Engineers figure out how to mass-produce chips packed with tiny diodes and transistors. Together, they launched our electronic age, and that's a big part of how computers shrank from room-sized to pocket-sized.

16.title: Engineering and Technology, The Tiniest Transistors
16.text:
Engineering and Technology, The Tiniest Transistors

Moore's law is the observation that the number of components on an integrated circuit doubles about every two years.

Computers get faster every year because microchips keep getting more densely packed with transistors. Early microchips had several thousand transistors. Today, a chip about the size of a fingernail holds billions.

In 1965, Gordon Moore noticed that the number of components on an integrated circuit had doubled about every year since they were invented. He predicted the trend would continue, and later revised the rate to every two years. This became Moore's law. Despite the name, it's not a physical law like Newton's laws. It's an observation and a prediction about technology.

How small can a transistor get? One team made one from a single atom. Using a scanning tunneling microscope, they arranged phosphorus atoms on etched silicon, covered them with hydrogen, then removed hydrogen atoms one by one to expose the phosphorus. A chemical reaction set the phosphorus into the silicon, and a new silicon layer protected it. The single phosphorus atoms could switch and amplify current. They're not practical yet, though. They're hard to make and only work at very low temperatures.
